title: Epileptic seizure: a temporal lobe seizure
description: There are many kinds of seizure. This episode shows one of the most common in adults: a seizure that begins deep in one temporal lobe and, as it spreads, takes awareness away for a minute or two. The person may stare, fumble or not respond, and often does not remember it. It is drawn starting on the left; in life it can start on either side. A seizure is abnormally intense, synchronised activity, so "more active" here does not mean working better.
caveat: This is unusually well-timed evidence for this project, because seizures are recorded directly with electrodes placed in the brain before epilepsy surgery, and with blood-flow scans injected during a seizure. But those recordings come from people whose epilepsy has not responded to medication, so they may not represent everyone. Where a seizure starts differs between people, and the starting zone can reach beyond the hippocampus and amygdala. The idea that the seizure switches off the brain's arousal systems, which in turn quietens the frontal and parietal cortex, is the researchers' hypothesis for why awareness is lost. What the brain does after the seizure ends is drawn as an assumption: the sources read describe the person's reduced responsiveness lasting several minutes, not the brain activity behind it.

phases.name: Onset
phases.caption: Fast, synchronised firing begins deep in one temporal lobe, in the hippocampus, the amygdala and the cortex around them. The person may still be aware at this point.

phases.name: Spread
phases.caption: The seizure activity spreads through the temporal lobe and across to the other side. Spread to both temporal lobes is greater in seizures where awareness is lost.

citations.title: Epileptogenicity of brain structures in human temporal lobe epilepsy: a quantified study from intracerebral EEG.
citations.quote: Statistically high EI values corresponded to structures involved early in the ictal process and producing rapid discharges at seizure onset.

citations.authors: Englot DJ, Yang L, Hamid H, Danielson N, Bai X, et al., Blumenfeld H
citations.title: Impaired consciousness in temporal lobe seizures: role of cortical slow activity.
citations.quote: propagation of unilateral mesial temporal fast seizure activity to the bilateral temporal lobes was significantly greater in complex-partial than in simple-partial seizures

phases.name: Awareness fades
phases.timescale: tens of seconds to a minute or two
phases.caption: Deep midline structures such as the thalamus become more active, and large areas of frontal and parietal cortex on both sides slow down, as in deep sleep. The seizure has not spread there; those areas have been quietened. This is when the person stops responding.

citations.quote: temporal lobe seizures associated with loss of consciousness produced CBF increases in the temporal lobe, followed by increases in bilateral midline subcortical structures

phases.name: Afterwards
phases.caption: The seizure stops. The person can stay confused or unresponsive for several minutes. What the brain is doing during that recovery is drawn here as a gradual return, which is an assumption.

order.rationale: The sources read describe behaviour after the seizure, reduced responsiveness for several minutes, not brain activity. The gradual return to rest is assumed.

regions.explanation: One of the deep temporal lobe structures where these seizures most often begin, according to electrode recordings in seventeen people before surgery. In every one of them more than one structure was involved at the start, and a review argues that the starting zone can extend beyond the hippocampus and amygdala.

regions.explanation: Frontal association cortex on both sides. Blood flow there drops sharply, and electrodes record slow waves like those of deep sleep, during seizures in which awareness is lost. The seizure itself has not spread here. The researchers propose that the seizure disrupts the brain's arousal systems, which then stop keeping this cortex awake; that explanation is a hypothesis. Drawn on the middle frontal gyrus; the finding is for frontal association cortex generally.
